title: Agentic attribution of cloud resource ownership: finding owners in the records you already keep
summary: Security teams spend nearly as much time hunting down resource owners as they do analyzing risk. Static tags and CMDB entries go stale the moment an engineer switches teams, leaving alert remediation stranded. But true ownership lives in the digital footprint people leave every day—Git commits, PR reviews, audit logs, and tickets. Our latest paper details an agentic architecture that mines these implicit signals across your existing tools to identify who actually builds, maintains, and answers for your cloud resources.
body_markdown:
- Our architecture found 92.1% of the weighted owners in a shared, verified pool, against 54.8% for Claude Code. Precision landed at 86.6% against 77.4%.
- It named a verified owner for 99 of 100 resources, and the coding agent got to 89.
- Coverage cost us $0.68 per unit of weighted recall, against $1.24 for the agent, a little over half.
- The gap comes from people who build and change resources without anyone writing their name down. We found them in Jira tickets and GitHub history.


Every security tool you run raises issues, and each one lands on a resource. Somebody has to fix it, and somebody has to answer for the resource it touches. AI agents can now investigate and rank those issues for you. But the last mile still runs through people, and most cloud environments can’t tell you who those people are. Our new paper tackles the routing problem head on.


## Where ownership actually lives


Ask a CMDB who owns a resource and you get whatever someone typed into an owner field, possibly years ago. Owners switch teams and hand work off, and the field ages with every move. Tags don’t fare better. In the organization we studied, nobody used the standard owner and team tags at all.


Yet the knowledge exists. People leave a trail every time they work: CloudTrail entries, Jira tickets, pull requests, commits, identity center roles.


We call it implicit ownership: ownership your records hold but the resource itself doesn’t. Recovering it means solving four problems at once:


1. **Scattered signal.** Each source holds a partial, sometimes stale trace, and none of them has the final word.
2. **Local conventions.** One company puts the owner in a tag and another hides it in ticket text, so fixed rules break between organizations.
3. **Multi-hop links.** A tag points to a deployment stack, the stack to a repo, the repo to pull requests, and the PR authors to a current employee.
4. **Uneven relationships** . The engineer who built a resource and someone who made one commit to a library it uses shouldn’t count the same.


## How the architecture works


We define ownership as a set of people and teams, each with one of five relation patterns that describe its tie to the resource. Explicit owner and direct work sit at the top, and the weaker patterns run down to peripheral mentions.


Service accounts and pipeline roles never count as owners. When a pipeline created the resource, the system follows the run to the commit or ticket behind it and finds the humans there.


The system then works in two phases:


- **Offline, once per organization.** Profiling agents study how your company records ownership and propose lookups, for example that a stack tag names a repo whose PR authors work on the resource. Code tests each lookup against your own data, and only lookups that reach people and generalize past their examples become tools. The agents also write an ownership playbook covering which tags you can trust and which leads go nowhere.
- **Online, per resource.** A coordinator agent reads the resource’s context first, so a load balancer with the name payments-api-prod-alb turns into search terms like payments and api for tickets and code.


Parallel investigator agents then chase open leads and register every role holder on a matching record, from assignee and reporter to author and reviewer. And the model never sets its own confidence score, so fixed rules combine evidence scores into one while code rejects any conclusion resting on evidence the agent never observed.


## What we measured


Nobody has a ground-truth ownership map, so we borrowed pooling from information retrieval research. Both systems’ candidates went into one pool, and a judge model checked every evidence piece against the live records.


Each verified owner then got a weight by relation pattern. Missing the person who built a resource costs ten times what missing a passing mention costs.


Both systems caught the person whose name sits on the resource, 47 and 48 of 49 explicit owners. The gap opened on direct work, the people who build, change, run and answer for a resource without a name tag to show for it.


Work records and code history explain most of it. GitHub evidence backs 46% of our verified owners and 2% of the agent’s, even though the agent had the GitHub CLI the whole time.


Recall also held where pre-computed signal ran thin, at 96% on thin resources and 94% where no lookup applied at all. Still, the agent found 32 people we didn’t propose, mostly weaker links through free-text ticket search, and our investigators had reached 11 of them along the way.


## What it means for your team


Ownership decides where every security issue lands. In Seemplicity’s[survey](https://go.seemplicity.io/hubfs/PDF%20Files%20(ebooks,%20files,%20docs,%20infographics)/Seemplicity_2026%20State%20of%20Exposure%20Management_Research%20Report.pdf) of 300 security and IT professionals, about half spend at least as much time coordinating remediation, owner hunting included, as they spend analyzing risk.


Owner fields and tags help only while somebody keeps them current. A system that reads your tickets, commits, audit logs and identity directories can name the people who build and run each resource, with the evidence attached.


We tested one organization on AWS, so we’ll keep pushing on new organizations, Azure, Google Cloud, and sources like CMDBs and on-call schedules. The full methodology lives in the paper so you can check our work.
